guides.title: Electricity & Circuits From Scratch
guides.summary: First principles of charge, current, voltage, resistance and power; what a circuit actually is; series vs parallel; reading schematics; using a multimeter; and the physics of electric shock.

sections.heading: Charge and current: the physical basis
sections.body: Electric charge, given the symbol Q and measured in coulombs, is a fundamental property of matter in the same way mass is. It comes in discrete lumps: the elementary charge is e = 1.602 x 10^-19 coulombs, an electron carries minus one of them and a proton plus one, and no isolated particle has ever been found with a fraction of that amount. One coulomb is therefore about 6.24 x 10^18 electrons, an absurdly large number, which tells you immediately that the coulomb is a human-scale unit built on an atomic-scale quantity. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, with a force given by Coulomb's law, F = k q1 q2 / r^2, where F is in newtons, the charges are in coulombs, r is their separation in metres, and the constant k is 8.988 x 10^9 newton metres squared per coulomb squared. That constant is enormous, which is why matter is electrically neutral almost everywhere: even a tiny imbalance of charge produces forces that immediately pull it back. Current, symbol I and measured in amperes, is simply the rate at which charge flows past a chosen point, I = dQ/dt, so one ampere is one coulomb per second. What actually moves in a metal is worth being precise about. In copper, each atom contributes roughly one loosely held valence electron to a shared sea of conduction electrons that belongs to the whole crystal rather than to any individual atom. Applying an electric field makes that sea drift, but the drift is astonishingly slow: in a two square millimetre copper wire carrying ten amperes the mean drift velocity is roughly 0.3 millimetres per second, so an individual electron would take over an hour to travel a metre. A lamp nonetheless lights the instant you close the switch, because what propagates is not the electrons but the electric field, travelling at a large fraction of the speed of light, 3.00 x 10^8 metres per second, and setting every free electron along the whole loop in motion almost simultaneously. The standard analogy is a pipe already full of water: opening the tap pushes water out of the far end immediately even though each individual molecule only crawls forward. Finally, one convention trips up nearly everyone. Conventional current is defined as flowing from positive to negative, the direction a positive charge would move, because Benjamin Franklin assigned the signs more than a century before the electron was discovered and guessed wrong. Electrons physically drift the other way, from negative to positive. Every schematic, every diode and transistor arrow, and every formula you will meet uses conventional current. Adopt it, use it consistently, and stop thinking about which way the electrons go.

sections.heading: Voltage, resistance and power, defined exactly
sections.body: Voltage, symbol V and measured in volts, is energy per unit charge: V = E/Q, so one volt is one joule per coulomb. The single most important thing to internalise is that voltage is always a difference between two points. There is no such thing as the voltage at a point in isolation; when someone says the voltage at pin three is 3.3 volts, they silently mean relative to the node everyone has agreed to call ground. The hydraulic analogy is genuinely useful here: voltage behaves like pressure difference, current like flow rate, and resistance like the narrowness of the pipe. Resistance, symbol R and measured in ohms, opposes current. For a uniform conductor it is set by geometry and material through R = rho L / A, where rho is the resistivity in ohm-metres, L is length in metres, and A is cross-sectional area in square metres. Double the length and you double the resistance; double the cross-section and you halve it. Resistivity spans an extraordinary range: copper is 1.68 x 10^-8 ohm metres, aluminium 2.65 x 10^-8, nichrome 1.10 x 10^-6, and glass somewhere between 10^10 and 10^14. Nichrome is about sixty-five times as resistive as copper, which is exactly why heating elements are made from it and wiring is not. Metals also have a positive temperature coefficient, meaning they conduct worse when hot: R(T) = R0 (1 + alpha (T - T0)), with alpha for copper equal to 0.00393 per degree Celsius. A copper motor winding at 100 degrees therefore has about 31 percent more resistance than the same winding at 20 degrees, which is why a motor draws noticeably less current once it has warmed up, and why a cold-start inrush current can be far higher than the running figure on the nameplate. Power, symbol P and measured in watts, is energy per second, and there are three algebraically equivalent expressions for it: P = VI, P = I^2 R, and P = V^2 / R. They are the same statement combined with Ohm's law, and you pick whichever form matches the two quantities you already know. Energy is simply power multiplied by time, E = Pt, and the kilowatt-hour used on electricity bills is one thousand watts for 3600 seconds, which is 3.6 x 10^6 joules. Work one example fully. A 12 volt heater element with a resistance of 4 ohms draws I = 12/4 = 3 amperes and dissipates P = 12 x 3 = 36 watts. Run for twenty minutes it consumes 36 watts times 1200 seconds, which is 43,200 joules, or 0.012 kilowatt-hours. Note that all 36 watts must leave the element as heat; if the element cannot shed that much, its temperature rises until either it does or something fails.

sections.heading: What a circuit is, and the three things it must have
sections.body: A circuit is a closed conductive loop running from a source's positive terminal, through a load, and back to its negative terminal. The word closed is doing all the work in that sentence. Break the loop anywhere at all and current stops everywhere in that loop, instantly and completely, because charge cannot accumulate indefinitely at the break. This is why a single failed switch, a corroded connector or one blown filament in a series string kills the whole thing regardless of how healthy the rest of it is. Every working circuit needs exactly three elements. It needs a source of electromotive force, usually shortened to emf, which may be a battery, generator, solar cell or power supply; emf is measured in volts and is the pump that does the work on the charge. It needs a conductive path, meaning wire, printed circuit board trace or metal chassis, ideally with resistance close enough to zero that it can be ignored. And it needs a load, something that converts electrical energy into another form: light, heat, mechanical motion or computation. A fourth element is not theoretically required but is practically indispensable, and that is protection, meaning a fuse or circuit breaker rated just above the intended working current so that a fault interrupts the loop before the wiring becomes an unintended heating element. Two failure states are constantly confused and the distinction matters enormously. An open circuit is a broken path: current is zero, nothing works, and the full source voltage appears across the break itself, which is why a disconnected mains conductor is still perfectly capable of killing you. A short circuit is the opposite, a near-zero-resistance path that bypasses the load entirely. Current in a short is limited only by the source's own internal resistance plus the resistance of the wiring, so it can reach hundreds or thousands of amperes within milliseconds. That is the mechanism behind almost every electrical fire, melted tool and vented lithium cell. Finally, ground deserves careful handling because the word carries two different meanings. In circuit analysis, ground is simply whichever node you have chosen to call zero volts so that every other voltage can be quoted against it. In a car that reference is the metal chassis itself, which is why only one wire needs to run out to each lamp. In building wiring, the protective earth is a physically real safety conductor bonded to the ground outside, and it is designed to carry no current at all under normal conditions. Treating signal ground and protective earth as interchangeable is a classic error and, on mains equipment, a genuinely dangerous one, because the safety conductor is sized and routed on the assumption that it will only ever carry fault current for the fraction of a second before a breaker opens, not the steady return current of a working load.

sections.heading: Series and parallel: the two fundamental topologies
sections.body: Almost every circuit you will ever meet reduces to combinations of two arrangements. In series, components are joined end to end so they share a single current path. Because there is nowhere else for charge to go, the current is identical through every element, so I total equals I1 equals I2 equals I3. The voltages across the elements add up to the source voltage, V total = V1 + V2 + V3, and the resistances add directly, R total = R1 + R2 + R3. The practical consequence is fragility: any element failing open, such as one blown bulb in an old-style Christmas string, kills the entire chain. In parallel, components share the same two nodes, so each has its own independent current path. Now the voltage is identical across every element, V total = V1 = V2 = V3, while the currents add, I total = I1 + I2 + I3. Conductances rather than resistances add, giving 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. For exactly two resistors there is a useful shortcut, R total = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2), and for n identical resistors the result is simply R/n. A sanity check worth burning into memory: a parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest branch resistance, because adding another path can only ever make it easier for current to flow. If your arithmetic produces a value larger than any individual resistor, you have made a mistake, almost always by forgetting to invert at the end. The great virtue of parallel wiring is independence: one element failing open leaves the others working, which is why house lighting, car lamps and the strings inside LED panels are wired this way. Now a worked example that appears everywhere in practice, the voltage divider. Put two resistors in series, R1 = 6.8 kilohms on top and R2 = 3.3 kilohms on the bottom, across a 9 volt supply. The series total is 10.1 kilohms, so the current is 9 divided by 10,100, which is 0.891 milliamperes. That same current flows through R2, so the voltage across it is 0.891 milliamperes times 3300 ohms, about 2.94 volts. The general rule is V out = V in times R2 / (R1 + R2), and it follows directly from the fact that series elements share a current. There is an important caveat: a divider is a weak source. The moment you connect a load whose resistance is comparable to R2, that load sits in parallel with R2, lowers the effective bottom resistance, and pulls the output voltage down. The usual rule of thumb is to make the load at least ten times R2, which keeps the error under about ten percent, or to buffer the divider with an op-amp follower when the output must not sag at all.

sections.heading: Reading schematics and measuring with a multimeter
sections.body: A schematic is a map of electrical connectivity, not of physical layout, and once you accept that it becomes far easier to read. Every line represents an ideal wire of zero resistance, so its length and route on the page mean nothing. A dot at a crossing means the two conductors are joined; no dot means one passes over the other with no connection, and because that distinction can be lost in a bad photocopy, careful draughtsmen avoid four-way junctions entirely. The core symbols are worth memorising: a battery is alternating long and short parallel lines, a resistor is a zigzag in the American convention or a plain rectangle in the IEC one, a capacitor is two parallel plates with the curved plate marking the negative side on polarised types, an LED is a triangle against a bar with two small arrows pointing away from it, and ground is a descending stack of shrinking horizontal bars. A digital multimeter is the instrument that turns a schematic into verified reality, and each of its functions connects to the circuit differently. Voltage is measured in parallel, with the probes placed across the component while the circuit is powered; a voltmeter presents a very high input impedance, typically ten megohms, so it draws almost no current and barely disturbs what it is measuring. Current is measured in series, which means you must physically break the circuit and insert the meter into the gap; an ammeter has near-zero resistance by design so that inserting it changes the current as little as possible. Resistance is measured with the power off and, wherever practical, with at least one leg of the component lifted out of circuit, because any parallel path through the rest of the board will read in combination and give you a misleadingly low value. The ohms function works by injecting the meter's own small test current, so applying it to a live circuit produces nonsense at best and damages the meter at worst. Continuity is the beep function, essentially a low-threshold resistance test, and it is the fastest way to check wires, fuses and switch contacts with the power off. One mistake dominates all others in both frequency and cost: leaving the red lead plugged into the ten-ampere current jack after a current measurement and then probing a voltage source. In that configuration the meter is a near-dead short across your supply. On a bench supply it blows the meter's internal fuse; on a car battery it can vaporise the probe tips and spray molten metal. Build a reflex: the instant a current measurement is finished, move the red lead back to the volts and ohms jack before doing anything else.

sections.heading: Safety: what actually hurts you, and standard practice
sections.body: It is current through the body that injures and kills, not voltage as such, but voltage is what drives that current, so the two cannot be separated in practice. For 50 or 60 hertz alternating current passing hand to hand, the approximate thresholds are well established. Around one milliampere is the threshold of perception, felt as a tingle. Around five milliamperes is painful but you can still let go. Between roughly ten and twenty milliamperes the let-go threshold is exceeded: the flexor muscles of the forearm are stronger than the extensors, so the hand clamps onto the conductor and you cannot release it voluntarily. Near thirty milliamperes respiratory paralysis begins, which is precisely why residual-current devices and ground-fault interrupters are set to trip there, or as low as four to six milliamperes for North American bathroom and kitchen outlets. Between roughly one hundred and two hundred milliamperes ventricular fibrillation becomes likely, and that is usually fatal without prompt defibrillation. Body resistance decides how much current a given voltage produces. Dry, intact skin hand to hand is typically somewhere between ten and one hundred kilohms, but wet, sweaty or broken skin can fall to about one kilohm. At one kilohm, 230 volts drives 230 milliamperes, which is firmly in the lethal band, while 12 volts drives only 12 milliamperes and is harmless through skin. That asymmetry is why supplies below about fifty volts are treated as extra-low voltage, but it must not be read as meaning low voltage is harmless in every respect: a 12 volt car battery can deliver six hundred amperes or more into a dropped spanner, causing severe burns, and the hydrogen it vents can be ignited by the resulting arc. Standard practice follows from all of this. Work on de-energised circuits wherever possible: lock out, tag out, then test with a meter you have just proved works on a known live source, because a meter that reads zero because it is faulty looks identical to one reading a genuinely dead circuit. Keep one hand in a pocket when probing anything live, so that a fault cannot drive current across your chest. Never work alone on mains. Discharge large capacitors in power supplies, microwave ovens and camera flash units through a suitable bleeder resistor before touching anything, since they retain lethal charge for minutes to hours after unplugging. Size fuses to protect the wire rather than the load: typical copper ampacities in free air are about three amperes for 0.5 square millimetres, ten for 1.0, and twenty for 2.5. And accept the legal reality that fixed mains wiring is a licensed activity in most jurisdictions. Learn on batteries and low-voltage supplies; hire an electrician for the building.

sections.heading: Alternating current, direct current, and why the grid runs on both
sections.body:
Every circuit analyzed so far assumed direct current (DC): charge flows in one direction, driven by a source of fixed polarity, like a battery. But plug a lamp into a wall outlet and something different is happening — the current is alternating (AC), reversing direction back and forth 60 times a second in North America (60 Hz) or 50 times a second across most of the rest of the world (50 Hz). The voltage traces a sine wave: v(t) = Vpeak·sin(ωt), where ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in radians per second. A "120 V" US outlet is not 120 V at every instant — that number is the RMS (root-mean-square) voltage, the DC-equivalent value that would deliver the same average power into a resistor. For a pure sinusoid, RMS = Vpeak/√2 ≈ 0.707·Vpeak, so a 120 V RMS outlet actually swings to about ±170 V peak. This is why a device rated "120 V AC" must tolerate momentary voltages far above 120 — its insulation and components are specified for the peak, not the RMS figure printed on the label.

The choice between AC and DC for the power grid was not inevitable — it was fought over, literally, in the late 1880s in what's remembered as the "War of the Currents." Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station (New York City, 1882) distributed DC at roughly 110 V, and it had a hard physical limit: DC at that voltage could only be economically distributed about a mile from the generating station, because line losses scale as I²R. To deliver a fixed amount of power P at low voltage, you need high current (P = VI, so I = P/V), and resistive loss in the transmission wire grows with the square of that current. George Westinghouse, backing Nikola Tesla's polyphase AC induction motor and, critically, the transformer, offered a way out: a transformer can step AC voltage up for transmission (low current, low I²R loss over miles of wire) and back down to a safe level at the point of use, because a transformer works by electromagnetic induction, which requires a changing magnetic flux — something steady DC cannot provide. No practical way existed in the 1880s to do the equivalent with DC. AC won the grid because of this one asymmetry, and it still runs the grid today, even though modern power electronics has since made long-haul HVDC (high-voltage DC) transmission viable for certain very long runs.

The arithmetic behind that century-old decision is worth doing once, because it explains every high-voltage transmission tower you'll ever see. Suppose a line with 2 Ω of total resistance must deliver 100 kW. At 100 V, the current required is I = P/V = 100,000/100 = 1000 A, and the resistive loss is I²R = 1000²×2 = 2,000,000 W — twenty times the power you're trying to deliver; the scheme is physically impossible, and the line voltage would simply collapse under the load. At 10,000 V (10 kV), the same 100 kW needs only I = 100,000/10,000 = 10 A, and the loss is I²R = 10²×2 = 200 W, just 0.2% of the delivered power. That hundred-fold jump in voltage bought a ten-thousand-fold reduction in loss, because loss depends on the square of current. This is the entire reason transmission lines run at tens or hundreds of kilovolts and step down through substations and pole transformers before reaching your house.

DC hasn't disappeared — it's actually what almost every electronic device wants internally (a phone, laptop, or LED needs a steady DC rail), which is why nearly every AC-powered gadget contains a rectifier (a diode bridge, covered in the components guide) to convert incoming AC back into DC. AC and DC aren't rivals inside a modern device; AC is the transport format, DC is what logic circuits and batteries actually consume.

sections.heading: What "ground" actually means — and why the third prong on a plug matters
sections.body:
"Ground" is one of the most overloaded words in electronics because it means two genuinely different things, and confusing them is a common source of both wiring mistakes and real electrical-shock hazard.

In circuit analysis, ground is just a reference node — an arbitrary point you declare to be 0 V so that every other voltage in the circuit can be stated as "so many volts relative to that point." It doesn't have to be, and often isn't, connected to the earth at all; a 9 V battery circuit sitting on a workbench can have its negative terminal labeled "ground" purely as bookkeeping, with no wire anywhere near actual dirt. This is sometimes called circuit common or signal ground to make clear it's a reference, not a physical connection to the planet.

Mains house wiring uses a second, physically real meaning: earth ground, a wire (usually bare copper or green-insulated) bonded to a metal stake driven into the earth (or building steel or a water pipe) at the electrical service panel. A standard US outlet has three contacts: hot (carries the alternating current from the utility), neutral (the return path, also bonded to earth — but only at the panel, not at the outlet), and ground (the third, round prong), which normally carries no current at all. Its only job is to be electrically connected to the metal chassis of whatever you plug in. Here's why that matters: imagine a fault inside a metal-cased appliance where a frayed hot wire touches the case. Without a ground wire, the case becomes energized at close to full line voltage and simply sits there — silently lethal — until a person touches it and the earth, at which point their body completes the circuit back to the source, and skin/body resistance is easily low enough at 120–240 V to pass a dangerous current. With the case bonded to ground, that same fault instead creates a near-dead-short from hot straight to earth through a very low-resistance path, drawing enough current to trip the circuit breaker or blow the fuse almost immediately — the appliance shuts itself off before anyone touches it. The third prong doesn't power anything; its entire purpose is to make faults fail loud and fast instead of quiet and lethal.

A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI in the US, RCD — residual-current device — elsewhere) is a further refinement required in bathrooms, kitchens, and outdoor outlets. It works by comparing the current flowing out on the hot wire to the current returning on the neutral wire, using a small differential transformer; in a healthy circuit those two currents are identical, since all current that leaves must return through the wiring. If even a small fraction — as little as 4–6 mA in US devices — leaks out some other path, such as through a person's body to earth, the transformer detects the imbalance and trips the circuit within milliseconds, well before the current reaches levels associated with cardiac risk. A GFCI is doing something an ordinary circuit breaker cannot: a breaker only responds to total current through the same wire pair exceeding a large threshold (like 15 or 20 A), which a shock current of tens or a few hundred milliamps through a person never comes close to tripping.

sections.heading: Building Your First Electronics Bench
sections.body: None of this requires a laboratory. A corner of a desk and a small kit of parts is enough to verify by hand every relationship in basic circuit theory, and the reason a bench matters is that measurement is what turns a formula from something you have read into something you believe. Each item earns its place for a specific reason. A solderless breadboard lets you build and unbuild a circuit in seconds; internally it is a grid of spring clips, with each short row of five holes connected together and the long rails down the sides connected along their length, and the two commonest beginner faults are forgetting that the centre channel splits the two halves of a row and assuming the power rails run unbroken when many boards break them at the midpoint. Resistors are the workhorse and you want a spread of values rather than many of one, because most exercises need a ratio rather than a particular number. A five percent tolerance part is fine for learning, but it does mean a nominal 470 ohm resistor may genuinely measure anywhere from 446 to 494 ohms, which is worth knowing before you blame your arithmetic for a mismatch. A quarter watt rating sets a real limit: at 9 volts across a single 100 ohm resistor the dissipation is 0.81 watts, more than three times the rating, and the part will scorch within seconds. The multimeter is the one item worth not economising on beyond a point, though a basic model covering DC and AC volts, ohms, continuity and diode test is genuinely sufficient. Solid-core jumper wire sits flat and stays put in a breadboard; stranded wire frays and pushes the clips apart. Batteries make better first sources than a bench supply because their limited current makes mistakes forgiving. Eye protection is not theatre: clipping a component lead launches a stiff offcut at eye height at surprising speed. And the log book is the item most people skip and most regret skipping.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (the common "830 tie-point" size is a good first choice; one with a metal backing plate is more rigid), from any electronics/hobby retailer
An assorted resistor kit (values from 10 Ω to 1 MΩ, 1/4 W, ±5% tolerance — often sold as a 300+ piece kit sorted by value)
A digital multimeter (DMM) with DC/AC voltage, resistance, continuity beep, and a diode-test setting — any basic model in the $15–30 range covers this
A pack of jumper wires (a pre-cut solid-core "breadboard wire kit," plus a set of flexible male-male jumpers)
A small assortment of standard 5mm LEDs (red, green, yellow) and a handful of basic silicon signal diodes
A bench power supply, or simply a battery holder set (a 9V clip and a couple of AA holders) as your first DC sources
Safety glasses — cheap, but non-negotiable once you start clipping component leads; clipped leads fly
A small pair of diagonal wire cutters and needle-nose pliers, from any hardware or electronics store
A notebook or spreadsheet to log predicted vs. measured values — the habit that turns tinkering into engineering

sections.heading: Breadboard, Predict, Then Measure: Verify Your First Circuit
sections.body: The single most useful habit in electronics is writing down a number before you measure it, because only then does a mismatch tell you anything. If you measure first, whatever the meter says will feel reasonable, and a wiring fault or a dead component can hide in plain sight for hours. The exercise below deliberately measures the same quantity two different ways, once indirectly by applying Ohm's law to the voltage across a known resistor, and once directly by breaking the loop and inserting the ammeter in series. Agreement between the two is strong evidence that both the circuit and your understanding of it are sound; disagreement localises the problem immediately. Expect about ten percent of scatter and do not chase it: a five percent resistor, a battery sagging under load because of its internal resistance, and an LED whose forward voltage drifts with current and temperature account for most of it. The final step pushes the current past the LED's rated maximum on purpose, on the cheapest component on the bench, because seeing a part run hot when the maths said it would is more persuasive than reading that current limiting matters.
steps: 1. On paper, sketch a simple loop: a 9 V battery, a 470 Ω resistor, and a red LED (forward voltage Vf ≈ 2.0 V, maximum current ≈ 20 mA) all in series.

2. Calculate the predicted current before touching any hardware: the resistor drops whatever voltage the battery and LED don't, so I = (9 V − 2.0 V) / 470 Ω ≈ 14.9 mA — safely under the LED's 20 mA maximum. Write this number down; you're about to check your own work against reality.

3. With the battery disconnected, build the loop on the breadboard: battery + to one leg of the resistor, the other leg to the LED's anode (longer lead), LED cathode (shorter lead, flat edge on the case) back to battery −.
4. Set the multimeter to DC voltage and connect the battery. Measure the voltage across the resistor alone, then the voltage across the LED alone.

5. Compute the current indirectly from the resistor's measured voltage using Ohm's law: I = V_measured / 470 Ω. Compare this to your 14.9 mA prediction — expect agreement within about ±10%, since a 5%-tolerance resistor and battery sag both introduce small error.

6. Now set the multimeter to its DC current (mA) range, break the loop at one point, and insert the meter in series to read current directly. Confirm it agrees with the value calculated indirectly in step 5 — this cross-check is exactly how you'll catch a wiring mistake or a failed component in real projects later.

7. Add a second 470 Ω resistor in parallel with the first (same two nodes) and re-measure the LED current. It should rise, since total resistance dropped — confirm it against R_parallel = (470×470)/(470+470) = 235 Ω, giving a predicted I ≈ (9−2)/235 ≈ 29.8 mA. At that current a standard LED may exceed its rated maximum and run hot — exactly the failure current-limiting resistors exist to prevent, worth seeing pushed slightly too far on a cheap LED so you respect the limit on everything more expensive afterward.

sections.heading: Beginner misconceptions that quietly wreck your intuition
sections.body: A handful of mental shortcuts feel true, are not, and cause more debugging misery than any gap in formulas. The first is the belief that current gets used up going round a circuit. It does not. In a simple series loop the current is identical at every point, full stop, and this follows directly from conservation of charge: if fifteen milliamperes left the battery and only ten came back, charge would be accumulating somewhere inside the circuit forever, which is physically impossible in a closed direct-current loop. What does get used up is energy, and it shows up as a voltage drop across each resistive element, not as a shrinking current. If you want a test of this, put an ammeter on either side of a lamp in a series loop; the two readings agree to within meter tolerance. The second misconception is that voltage travels along wires and is consumed by their length, or that a thicker wire somehow carries a higher voltage. Ordinary hookup wire has so little resistance, roughly 0.05 ohms for a metre of 22-gauge copper, that the drop along it is negligible beside the drops across resistors, LEDs and motors. Essentially all of a circuit's voltage drop occurs across its components, not its connections. The water analogy, in which charge is water, voltage is pressure and resistance is a narrowing of the pipe, is genuinely useful but breaks down precisely here: real wire under hobby conditions is not a leaky pipe losing pressure with distance. The honest caveat is that this stops being true at high current or long runs, where wire resistance is exactly why a starter cable is thumb-thick and why a long extension lead can dim what it feeds. The third misconception concerns speed, and it surprises people most. The individual electrons drifting through copper move on the order of millimetres per second at ordinary currents, slower than a snail, yet a light comes on apparently instantly. The resolution is that current is not electrons sprinting from the switch to the bulb. Closing the switch establishes an electric field throughout the whole circuit, and that field propagates at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, commonly between fifty and ninety-nine percent of it depending on conductor geometry and insulation, which is the same physics that sets signal delay in long cables. Every free electron in the loop starts moving at nearly the same moment. The electrons that light your filament were already sitting in it before you touched the switch; you did not send them, you simply told all of them, everywhere at once, to start moving together. Holding that picture correctly matters practically, because it is what makes cable length, signal timing and the behaviour of long runs comprehensible rather than mysterious.

guides.title: Ohm's & Kirchhoff's Laws With Worked Examples
guides.summary: The three equations that solve nearly every DC circuit - Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's current law and Kirchhoff's voltage law - with full worked solutions, systematic node and mesh analysis, Thevenin equivalents, and the mistakes that produce wrong answers.

sections.heading: Ohm's law: statement, scope and limits
sections.body: Ohm's law states that for an ohmic conductor held at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the voltage across it, which is written V = I R, or equivalently I = V/R and R = V/I. Here V is the potential difference across the element in volts, I is the current through it in amperes, and R is its resistance in ohms. The three forms are one relation rearranged, and the familiar memory triangle puts V on top with I and R side by side beneath it, so covering the quantity you want leaves the expression that gives it. Two habits prevent most errors in applying it. The first is being clear about which two terminals the voltage is across and which branch the current is through: the law connects the voltage across a particular element to the current through that same element, and mixing an element's current with the whole circuit's voltage is the commonest way to get a plausible but wrong answer. The second is converting to base SI units before substituting, since kilohms and milliamperes cancel neatly only if you are careful. It is important to understand that Ohm's law is an empirical property of certain materials, not a universal law of physics in the way conservation of charge is. It holds well for metals, carbon composition and film resistors, and most electrolytes across their rated operating range. It fails outright for several everyday components. In diodes and LEDs, current rises roughly exponentially with voltage, as described by the Shockley equation, so the ratio V over I changes by orders of magnitude across the operating range and is not a meaningful resistance at all. In incandescent lamps the tungsten filament's resistance climbs several-fold as it heats, so a 60 watt bulb that measures around 20 ohms cold behaves as roughly 240 ohms once running at 120 volts, which is why filament lamps draw a large inrush current at switch-on and usually fail at that instant. Thermistors, varistors, gas discharge tubes and every semiconductor junction are similarly non-ohmic. For any of these, the useful quantity is the dynamic or small-signal resistance, r = dV/dI, meaning the local slope of the device's characteristic curve at the actual operating point, rather than the chord V/I from the origin. Finally, always pair Ohm's law with the power relations P = VI = I squared R = V squared over R, because a resistor chosen only for its resistance will burn. A 100 ohm resistor across 12 volts passes 120 milliamperes and dissipates 1.44 watts; a common quarter-watt part will char and drift permanently within seconds, so the job needs a 2 watt part or larger.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) - conservation of charge
sections.body: Kirchhoff's current law states that the algebraic sum of the currents entering any node equals the sum of the currents leaving it. Written the other way, if you count currents leaving as negative, the sum of all currents at a node is zero. A node is any point where two or more components connect, and every point along an unbroken wire is electrically the same node, which matters more than beginners expect: a sprawling web of wire joining five components is one node, and treating each solder joint as a separate node produces equations that are redundant rather than wrong but waste a great deal of effort. The law is nothing more than conservation of charge applied locally. Charge cannot pile up at a junction of ideal wires, because any accumulation would immediately produce an electric field opposing further accumulation, so whatever flows in must flow out. Take a concrete case. Three wires meet at node A. Wire one carries 5.0 amperes into the node and wire two carries 1.8 amperes in. The third is unknown, so I3 must be 5.0 plus 1.8, which is 6.8 amperes out of the node. If your algebra returns a negative number for an unknown current, that is not an error and should not be corrected by hand; it simply means the true current flows opposite to the direction you arbitrarily assumed when setting up the problem. Sign conventions are a bookkeeping choice, and the mathematics reports the physical direction back to you. In practice the law explains why adding a parallel branch never reduces the voltage available to the existing branches but does increase the total current the supply must provide. Add a fourth LED strip drawing 0.9 amperes to a rail already carrying 2.4 amperes and the supply must now deliver 3.3 amperes; if it cannot, its output voltage sags and every branch dims together, which is a symptom people frequently misdiagnose as a fault in the newly added strip. The law is also the fastest fault-finding tool available. If the current entering a section of a system does not equal the current leaving it, the difference is going somewhere it should not: through moisture tracking, damaged insulation, or a partially shorted component. That is precisely the operating principle of a residual-current device or ground-fault interrupter, which compares the current in the live conductor with the current returning in the neutral and trips when the imbalance exceeds a threshold, commonly 30 milliamperes, because the missing current is by definition flowing through the earth or through a person. The same reasoning generalises: any time two measurements of what should be one current disagree, the difference has a physical path, and finding that path is the fault. A clamp meter placed around both conductors of a healthy cable reads zero for exactly this reason, since the outgoing and returning currents cancel; a nonzero reading is a leakage measurement, not a wiring quirk.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) - conservation of energy
sections.body: Kirchhoff's voltage law states that around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of all potential differences is zero. Equivalently, the sum of the voltage rises equals the sum of the voltage drops. This is conservation of energy stated for a circuit: a unit of charge carried all the way around a loop and returned to its starting point must have experienced no net change in energy, because it has arrived back where it began. Sign discipline is the whole difficulty of applying it, and the fix is to adopt a single rule and never deviate mid-problem. First choose a direction to walk the loop, conventionally clockwise. Second, traversing a source from its negative terminal to its positive terminal is a rise, entered as plus V, and from positive to negative is a drop, entered as minus V. Third, traversing a resistor in the same direction as your assumed current is a drop, entered as minus I times R, and against that assumed current is a rise, plus I times R. Work a single loop fully. A 9 volt battery with an internal resistance of 0.5 ohms drives R1 = 100 ohms and R2 = 220 ohms in series. Walking clockwise gives 9 minus I times 0.5 minus I times 100 minus I times 220 equals zero, so 9 equals I times 320.5, and I = 0.02808 amperes, or 28.08 milliamperes. Now check the answer by computing each drop separately: the internal resistance drops 0.0141 volts, R1 drops 2.808 volts, and R2 drops 6.178 volts. Those sum to 9.000 volts, exactly the source. Perform this check every time, without exception; it catches very nearly every arithmetic slip, and it costs seconds. A second check worth building into the same habit is a power audit. Total power delivered here is 9 times 0.02808, which is 0.2527 watts. Dissipation in R2 is I squared times R, or 0.02808 squared times 220, which is 0.1735 watts. That makes a quarter-watt resistor marginal in this position, running at almost 70 percent of its rating where it will get hot enough to drift in value and to discolour a circuit board, so a half-watt part is the correct choice. Note also what the internal resistance did: it consumed only 14 millivolts here because the current is small, but the same cell delivering half an ampere would lose a quarter of a volt internally, which is the mechanism behind a battery that measures fine unloaded yet fails to run the device. One conceptual caveat deserves stating honestly: the law as written holds for circuits small enough, or slow enough, that no significant magnetic flux is changing through the loop. Where a changing flux threads the loop, as in a transformer winding or a fast digital circuit with a large loop area, an induced voltage appears that belongs to no component, and the naive sum around the loop no longer reaches zero. For direct-current work at ordinary scales the effect is negligible, but it is the reason careful high-speed layout keeps signal and return paths close together, minimising loop area.

sections.heading: Node-voltage analysis - the systematic method
sections.body: Node-voltage analysis solves any resistive network mechanically, which is its great virtue: it needs no cleverness and no recognition of special cases, so it works when a circuit is too tangled for series-parallel reduction. The procedure has four steps. Identify every node, then pick one to be ground at zero volts, choosing the node with the most connections because that choice minimises the algebra. Label the remaining node voltages V1, V2 and so on; these are your unknowns, and there is one equation to come for each of them. Write Kirchhoff's current law at each unknown node, expressing every branch current using Ohm's law in the form (V of this node minus V of the other node) divided by R. Then solve the simultaneous equations. Work an example. A 12 volt source connects through R1 = 1 kilohm to node A. From node A, R2 = 2 kilohms runs to ground and R3 = 3 kilohms also runs to ground. Applying the current law at A, with current in on the left and current out on the right, gives (12 minus V_A) over 1000 equals V_A over 2000 plus V_A over 3000. Multiplying through by 6000 clears the denominators: 6 times (12 minus V_A) equals 3 V_A plus 2 V_A, so 72 minus 6 V_A equals 5 V_A, giving 72 equals 11 V_A and V_A = 6.545 volts. Verify it independently using the divider shortcut, which is available here because the topology happens to be simple: R2 in parallel with R3 is 2000 times 3000 over 5000, which is 1200 ohms, so V_A = 12 times 1200 over (1000 plus 1200) = 12 times 0.5455 = 6.545 volts. The two routes agree, which is the point of doing both. Recovering the branch currents completes the picture: through R1 the current is (12 minus 6.545) over 1000 = 5.455 milliamperes, through R2 it is 6.545 over 2000 = 3.273 milliamperes, and through R3 it is 6.545 over 3000 = 2.182 milliamperes. The current law check is that 3.273 plus 2.182 equals 5.455, which it does. Mesh analysis is the dual method, assigning a circulating current to each independent loop and writing the voltage law for each. The practical rule for choosing between them is simply to count: use node analysis when the circuit has fewer independent nodes than loops, and mesh analysis when the reverse holds, because whichever gives fewer simultaneous equations is less work and offers fewer chances to make a sign error. One complication is worth knowing in advance. An ideal voltage source connected directly between two non-reference nodes fixes the difference between them but leaves its own current unknown, so you cannot write an ordinary current equation at either node alone. The standard remedy is the supernode: enclose both nodes in one boundary, apply the current law to everything crossing that boundary, and supply the missing relation from the source itself, which states that one node voltage equals the other plus the source voltage. That gives two equations for two unknowns again, which is the balance every systematic method depends on.

sections.heading: Thevenin equivalent - collapsing a network to two components
sections.body: Thevenin's theorem says that any linear two-terminal network of sources and resistors, no matter how complicated inside, is exactly equivalent as seen from those two terminals to a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistor R_th. Exactly equivalent means that no measurement made at the terminals can distinguish the real network from its equivalent, which is why the theorem is so useful: it lets you replace everything upstream of a load with two components and then reason about the load in one line. The procedure is three steps. V_th is the open-circuit voltage measured at the terminals with the load removed. R_th is the resistance looking back into those terminals with all independent sources deactivated, meaning voltage sources replaced by a short circuit, since an ideal voltage source holds zero volts across itself when deactivated, and current sources replaced by an open circuit, since an ideal current source passes zero amperes when deactivated. The load current then follows as I_load = V_th divided by (R_th plus R_load). Work a case. A 15 volt source feeds R1 = 4.7 kilohms to an output node, and R2 = 10 kilohms runs from that node to ground. What does the output do when driving a 2.2 kilohm load? With no load, V_th = 15 times 10000 over (4700 plus 10000) = 15 times 0.6803 = 10.20 volts. Deactivating the source shorts the top of R1 to ground, putting R1 and R2 in parallel, so R_th = 4700 times 10000 over 14700 = 3197 ohms. With the 2.2 kilohm load attached, I = 10.20 over (3197 plus 2200) = 1.890 milliamperes, and V_out = 1.890 milliamperes times 2200 ohms = 4.16 volts. The unloaded 10.20 volts has collapsed to 4.16 volts, a sag of 59 percent. That is the quantitative version of the warning that a resistive divider is a weak source, and the working rule that follows is to keep the load resistance at least ten times R_th if you want the sag under about ten percent. Maximum power transfer drops straight out of the same framework: a load absorbs the greatest power when R_load equals R_th, but at that point efficiency is only 50 percent, because the source's own internal resistance dissipates exactly as much as the load does. That trade is correct for signal matching in antennas and audio lines, and wrong for delivering power, where you want R_th as small as you can make it. There is a second, purely practical way to obtain the same two numbers on a bench without any analysis at all, and it is worth knowing because it works on a circuit whose insides you cannot see. Measure the open-circuit voltage at the terminals, which is V_th directly. Then load the terminals with a resistor small enough to pull the output down noticeably and compute R_th from the sag: R_th equals R_load times (V_open minus V_loaded) divided by V_loaded. If the open-circuit reading is 10.20 volts and a 2.2 kilohm load brings it to 4.16 volts, that returns 2200 times 6.04 over 4.16, about 3195 ohms, matching the calculated figure. Keep the test load modest enough that nothing inside is driven beyond its linear range or power rating.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and a verification checklist
sections.body: Certain errors account for the large majority of wrong answers, and it is worth knowing them by name. The most frequent is mixing units: 4.7 kilohms is 4700 ohms, 22 milliamperes is 0.022 amperes, and 100 nanofarads is 1 times 10 to the minus 7 farads. Convert everything to base SI units before substituting and convert back only at the end, because mixed prefixes produce answers wrong by exact powers of ten, which look plausible enough to survive a casual glance. The second is adding parallel resistors directly. The relation is that the reciprocals add, 1 over R_total equals the sum of 1 over each R, and forgetting the final reciprocal is the single commonest slip in all of circuit arithmetic: people compute 1 over R_total and then report that number as the resistance. The sanity check is that a parallel combination is always smaller than its smallest branch. The third is assuming voltage is used up along a wire. An ideal wire has no drop and both its ends are the same node, but real wire does drop, and in low-voltage high-current work you must budget for it. Ten metres of 1.0 square millimetre copper, counting both the out and return conductors as twenty metres, has a resistance of 1.68 times 10 to the minus 8, times 20, divided by 1 times 10 to the minus 6, which is 0.336 ohms; at 5 amperes that wastes 1.68 volts and 8.4 watts as heat in the cable. The fourth is inconsistent sign conventions when walking a loop, curable only by adopting one traversal rule and applying it rigidly. The fifth is ignoring a source's internal resistance: a tired AA cell can have an ohm or more, so at 500 milliamperes it loses half a volt inside itself, which is exactly why it reads a healthy 1.5 volts on a meter yet will not run the device. The sixth is sizing a resistor by resistance alone without checking P = I squared R. Once a circuit is solved, run a five-point verification. Do all node voltages lie between the supply rails, since a passive network cannot produce a node above the positive rail or below ground? Does the current law balance at every node? Does the voltage law close to zero around at least two independent loops? Does the total power dissipated in the resistors equal the total power delivered by the sources? And are the numbers physically sane, with no resistor asked to dissipate beyond its rating and no conductor asked to carry more than its ampacity? A final habit worth building is an order-of-magnitude estimate made before any detailed algebra, since a rough answer computed in your head is what makes a factor-of-ten slip obvious the moment the exact result appears.

sections.heading: Mesh-current analysis — the loop-based dual of node-voltage
sections.body:
Node-voltage analysis solves a circuit by finding unknown node voltages; mesh-current analysis is its mirror image, solving instead for a fictitious circulating current assigned to each independent loop ("mesh," meaning a loop containing no other loop inside it — a windowpane in a planar circuit diagram). Where node-voltage naturally has one equation per non-reference node, mesh-current has one equation per mesh, and for a circuit with more independent loops than it has nodes, mesh analysis is usually the shorter path to a solution — pick whichever method gives you fewer simultaneous equations.

The method: draw each mesh current (I₁, I₂, …) circulating in the same direction around its window (clockwise is conventional). Any branch shared between two meshes carries the difference of the two mesh currents flowing through it. Then write one KVL equation per mesh, summing voltage rises and drops around that loop exactly as in single-loop KVL, expressing every resistor drop in terms of whichever mesh current(s) actually flow through that branch. Once you solve the resulting system for I₁, I₂, …, every real branch current is recoverable as a sum or difference of the mesh currents that pass through it, and every voltage follows from there via Ohm's law.

Worked example: a two-mesh circuit has, in its left window, a 10 V source in series with a 2 Ω resistor (R₁); its right window has a 5 V source in series with a 3 Ω resistor (R₃); the two windows share a middle branch containing a 4 Ω resistor (R₂), through which the shared current is (I₁ − I₂) when both mesh currents circulate clockwise. Writing KVL clockwise around each loop:

Left mesh: 10 − I₁(2) − (I₁−I₂)(4) = 0 → 6I₁ − 4I₂ = 10
Right mesh: 5 − I₂(3) − (I₂−I₁)(4) = 0 → −4I₁ + 7I₂ = 5

Solving simultaneously (by substitution, or via the determinant method): the system determinant is (6)(7) − (−4)(−4) = 42 − 16 = 26, giving I₁ = [(10)(7) − (−4)(5)] / 26 = 90/26 ≈ 3.46 A and I₂ = [(6)(5) − (−4)(10)] / 26 = 70/26 ≈ 2.69 A. The current through the shared 4 Ω resistor is I₁ − I₂ ≈ 0.77 A, flowing from the left loop into the right loop. This problem didn't resolve to tidy integers, which is normal — real circuits rarely do, and it's exactly why the systematic matrix approach matters more than mental arithmetic once you're past textbook-simple topologies.

Two cautions round out the method. Mesh analysis in its plain form assumes a planar circuit, one drawable with no wires crossing, since only then are the windows well defined; a non-planar network needs the general loop-current formulation or node analysis instead. The second concerns an ideal current source in a branch shared between two meshes: its voltage is unknown, so no ordinary voltage-law equation can be written through it. The remedy is the supermesh — walk one larger loop around the outside of both meshes, avoiding that branch, and take the missing equation from the source itself, which fixes the difference between the two mesh currents.

sections.heading: Superposition — solving a multi-source circuit one contributor at a time
sections.body:
Superposition is the theorem that lets you split a hard problem — a linear circuit with several independent sources acting at once — into several easy problems, each with only one source active, and then simply add the results. It's valid because resistors, and the KCL/KVL equations built from them, are linear: doubling an input doubles the response, and the response to a sum of inputs equals the sum of the responses to each input alone. It does not apply to circuits containing nonlinear elements like diodes or transistors in their general operating region — only to networks of purely linear components.

The procedure: to find the response due to one source, deactivate every other independent source — replace every other independent voltage source with a short circuit (0 V, a plain wire) and every other independent current source with an open circuit (0 A, removed entirely) — then solve the now-simpler circuit normally. Repeat for each source in turn, then algebraically sum the individual contributions, respecting sign and direction, to get the total.

Worked example: node A is fed by two independent sources in parallel and loaded by a resistor R = 4 Ω to ground. Branch 1 is a 12 V source in series with R₁ = 2 Ω, feeding node A. Branch 2 is an ideal 3 A current source injecting directly into node A. Find the total voltage at node A.

Step 1 — only the 12 V source active (open the 3 A current source, removing that branch): the circuit collapses to a simple series loop of the 12 V source, R₁ = 2 Ω, and R = 4 Ω. Current = 12/(2+4) = 2 A, so this contribution alone produces 2 A × 4 Ω = 8 V at node A.

Step 2 — only the 3 A source active (short the 12 V source, putting R₁ = 2 Ω in parallel with R = 4 Ω, both now running from node A to ground): the 3 A splits by the current-divider rule; the share through R is 3 A × [R₁/(R₁+R)] = 3 × (2/6) = 1 A, giving a contribution of 1 A × 4 Ω = 4 V.

Total voltage at node A = 8 V + 4 V = 12 V, and total current through R = 12/4 = 3 A — which checks against summing the two individual R-currents directly (2 A + 1 A = 3 A). Superposition doesn't just work here; the fact that both routes to the answer agree is exactly the self-check that should become a habit whenever you use it.

One caution catches people who have otherwise understood the method: superposition applies to voltages and currents, which are linear in the sources, but never to power. Power goes as the square of current, and the square of a sum is not the sum of squares, so adding per-source dissipations gives a wrong answer. Here the resistor carries 2 A from one contribution and 1 A from the other; squaring separately and adding yields (4 + 1) × 4 Ω = 20 W, while the true figure uses the actual 3 A total and is 9 × 4 = 36 W. Combine into the real branch current first, then compute power once.

sections.heading: Norton equivalents, source transformation, and the maximum-power-transfer trap
sections.body:
Just as any linear two-terminal network can be collapsed to a Thevenin equivalent (a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistance R_th), it can equally be collapsed to a Norton equivalent: a single current source I_N in parallel with the same resistance, now called R_N (R_N = R_th always, since it's the identical resistance seen from the terminals — only the source form differs). The two are related by source transformation: I_N = V_th / R_th, and conversely V_th = I_N × R_N. Being able to flip a stubborn voltage-source-in-series branch into a current-source-in-parallel branch, or back, is often the fastest way to combine two sources that are awkwardly oriented relative to each other, letting you merge them algebraically before doing any real analysis.

A theorem that falls straight out of the Thevenin/Norton framework is maximum power transfer: given a source with fixed Thevenin resistance R_th driving a variable load R_L, the power delivered to the load is maximized when R_L = R_th. This is provable directly from calculus — with I = V_th/(R_th+R_L) and P_L = I²R_L, differentiating with respect to R_L and setting the result to zero yields exactly R_L = R_th — but the number worth remembering is what happens at that maximum: exactly half the total power generated is dissipated in the source's own internal resistance, so efficiency at the point of maximum power transfer is only 50%.

This is where engineers new to the theorem get tripped up: maximum power transfer is not the same goal as maximum efficiency, and for most real power systems you want efficiency, not the theorem's matched condition. Take a source with V_th = 10 V and R_th = 50 Ω (a plausible output impedance for a small audio amplifier or RF source). At the matched load R_L = 50 Ω: I = 10/100 = 0.1 A, delivered power P_L = 0.1²×50 = 0.5 W, and total power drawn is 0.1²×100 = 1 W — efficiency 0.5/1 = 50%, half a watt wasted as heat inside the source for every half watt reaching the load. Now try R_L = 200 Ω: I = 10/250 = 0.04 A, P_L = 0.04²×200 = 0.32 W — less delivered power than the matched case, as expected — but total power is 0.04²×250 = 0.4 W, giving efficiency 0.32/0.4 = 80%. This is exactly why a battery charger, a wall power supply, or a solar charge controller is deliberately designed with the load resistance far higher than the source's internal resistance, not matched to it — chasing efficiency, where matched-impedance thinking would waste half your energy as heat. Impedance matching earns its keep in low-power signal and RF work (audio lines, antenna feeds), where getting the maximum signal through matters more than a wasted fraction of a milliwatt; it's close to the opposite of the right instinct anywhere real power — batteries, mains, motors — is involved.

sections.heading: What You Need to Verify These Laws on a Real Bench
sections.body: Circuit theory stops being abstract the moment you build the exact network an equation describes and read the answer off a meter, and a very small amount of equipment is enough to do that for every law in direct-current analysis. Each item on the list is there for a specific reason. The multimeter needs both a direct-current voltage range and a direct-current milliampere range, because the two are used differently: voltage is measured in parallel with the circuit intact, while current requires you to break the branch and insert the meter in series, and the ability to cross-check a current computed from a voltage against a current measured directly is what makes a verification meaningful rather than circular. The resistor values suggested are deliberately not round multiples of one another, because networks built from four identical resistors have symmetries that can hide a sign error or a swapped branch; awkward ratios force the arithmetic to be genuinely tested. Two independent sources are needed for the superposition and multi-source exercises, and they must be genuinely independent, meaning two separate batteries or a dual-output supply rather than two taps off one divider, since a shared source is not two sources. Batteries have a hidden virtue here: their internal resistance is large enough to be measurable, so the gap between the predicted and measured result gives you a direct handle on a quantity textbooks usually treat as a footnote. Alligator-clip leads matter more than they look; probing a node by hand while reading a display and holding a notebook is how slipped probes short adjacent pins, and a clip that stays put also keeps the connection resistance constant between readings. The calculator or spreadsheet should be set up in advance to solve two-by-two and three-by-three simultaneous systems, whether by substitution or by determinants, because the friction of solving a system by hand is the main reason people skip the prediction and just measure. And the notebook is the item that turns the exercise into evidence: a predicted value written before power is applied, sitting beside the measured value, is the only arrangement in which a disagreement becomes information rather than something you rationalise away. Expect around five to ten percent of scatter from resistor tolerance and meter accuracy stacked together, and treat anything larger as a real discrepancy worth tracking down rather than noise.
ingredients: A digital multimeter (DMM) with DC voltage and DC current (mA) ranges, from any electronics/hobby store
A breadboard and a small assortment of resistors (values like 1 kΩ, 2.2 kΩ, 3.3 kΩ, 4.7 kΩ let you build clean multi-branch networks)
Two independent DC sources — a bench power supply is ideal, or two separate batteries (e.g., a 9V and a 6V pack of four AA cells) with holders
Jumper wires and a set of alligator-clip test leads for tapping into a live circuit without disturbing it
A calculator or spreadsheet set up to solve 2×2 or 3×3 simultaneous equations, by hand substitution or matrix/Cramer's-rule entry, so predictions can be checked quickly
A notebook to record predicted vs. measured values at every node and branch — the discrepancy is often more instructive than the agreement

sections.heading: Verify KCL, KVL and Node-Voltage Predictions on a Real Circuit
sections.body: The exercise below converts three laws from statements you have read into results you have personally confirmed with a meter, and its structure is deliberate: every quantity is obtained twice, by calculation and by measurement, so the two can be compared. Order matters. Solving for the node voltage before applying power is not a formality; measure first and whatever the meter reads will feel reasonable, letting a swapped resistor or misread colour band pass unnoticed. A written prediction commits you to a number reality can contradict. When the currents are compared at the node, expect agreement to within roughly five to ten percent rather than exactly, because three resistors at five percent tolerance and a meter with its own accuracy specification stack up to about that much; a mismatch of thirty percent or more is not tolerance and means something is genuinely wrong, most often a branch landing on the wrong breadboard row. When the loop is walked for the voltage law, consistency of polarity is the whole trick: keep the black probe on the point you are walking from and the red on the point you are walking to, so the meter's own sign does the bookkeeping and the readings sum to zero rather than to twice one drop. One honest caveat about the source: a battery's terminal voltage falls under load because of its internal resistance, so measure the supply while the circuit is running and use that loaded figure. Changing one resistor and predicting the new result before measuring is the step that matters most, since it rehearses the working method on a circuit you may not be able to probe next time.
steps: 1. Build a simple three-branch network on the breadboard meeting at one node: a 9 V source through R1 = 2.2 kΩ into node A, a second resistor R2 = 3.3 kΩ from node A to ground, and a third resistor R3 = 4.7 kΩ from node A to ground as a parallel load branch.

2. Before connecting power, solve for node A's voltage by hand using the node-voltage method — sum the currents leaving node A through each branch, set the sum to zero, and solve the single resulting equation for V_A. Write down the predicted value.
3. Connect the circuit and measure V_A directly with the DMM's DC voltage range (black probe to ground, red probe to node A).
4. Measure the voltage across each individual resistor and, using Ohm's law with each resistor's known value, back-calculate the current through each of the three branches.

5. Add up the currents flowing into node A and the currents flowing out. They should match to within about 5–10% (the tolerance stack of three 5%-tolerance resistors plus meter accuracy) — your own hands-on confirmation of Kirchhoff's Current Law.

6. Measure voltage drops all the way around one complete loop of the circuit (source, R1, R3, back to source) with the meter, keeping consistent polarity, and sum them algebraically. They should sum to zero, or very close to it — your confirmation of Kirchhoff's Voltage Law.

7. Swap R3 for a different value (say 10 kΩ) and predict the new V_A before measuring again. This rehearses the real workflow: predict, then verify, then trust the prediction on the next circuit you can't as easily probe.

guides.title: Components: Resistors, Capacitors, Diodes & Transistors
guides.summary: What each fundamental electronic component does, the governing equations, how to read markings and choose ratings, canonical circuits (LED driver, RC filter, rectifier, switch, amplifier), and the failure modes that destroy them.

sections.heading: Resistors - values, codes and ratings
sections.body:
A resistor's only job is to oppose the flow of charge, converting the energy it absorbs into heat. Inside a typical film part a thin resistive layer is deposited on a ceramic rod and laser-cut into a spiral to lengthen the current path until the target resistance is reached; electrons drifting through that layer collide with the atomic lattice, and each collision turns directed motion into vibration, which is heat. Two equations govern everything a resistor does. Ohm's law, V = I x R, gives the voltage across the part as the current through it multiplied by its resistance in ohms. The power law, P = I^2 x R, equivalently P = V^2 / R, gives how fast that heat is produced, in watts. Together they support the two everyday jobs: limiting current to a value the rest of the circuit can survive, and dividing a voltage into a predictable fraction of itself.

Values are not arbitrary. Manufacturers stock the E-series, spaced logarithmically so that consecutive values, widened by their tolerance bands, just touch without leaving gaps. E12 (10 percent tolerance) gives twelve values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68 and 82. E24 (5 percent) interleaves 11, 13, 16, 20, 24, 30, 36, 43, 51, 62, 75 and 91. E96 (1 percent) offers ninety-six. This matters practically: if a calculation asks for 327 ohms you will not find one, and the design must tolerate the nearest stocked 330.

The four-band colour code prints the value on the body. Band one is the first digit, band two the second, band three a power-of-ten multiplier, band four the tolerance. Digit colours run black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9; tolerance is gold for 5 percent, silver 10 percent, brown 1 percent, red 2 percent. Yellow-violet-red-gold therefore reads 4, 7, x100 - 4,700 ohms, or 4.7 kilohm, at 5 percent. Five-band precision parts carry three significant digits before the multiplier. Surface-mount parts use numeric codes instead: 472 means 47 x 10^2 = 4.7 kilohm; 4R7 means 4.7 ohms, the letter R standing in for the decimal point; the four-digit code 4701 means 470 x 10^1.

Three further ratings decide whether a part survives. Power handling for through-hole parts runs 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 and 5 watts; surface-mount 0402 is about 0.063 W, 0603 about 0.1 W, 0805 about 0.125 W and 1206 about 0.25 W. Derate to half the nameplate figure for long life. Voltage rating is a separate and independent limit: a quarter-watt through-hole part is typically rated 250 V, and exceeding that arcs across the body however little power is flowing. Temperature coefficient describes drift with heat, roughly 50 to 100 parts per million per degree Celsius for metal film, 200 to 1,500 for carbon film, and 25 or better for a precision reference. Familiar variants extend the same idea: a potentiometer is a three-terminal adjustable divider; a thermistor changes resistance with temperature, the NTC type falling as it warms, which is why one in series with a supply limits switch-on inrush; and a shunt is a deliberately tiny value such as 0.1 ohm used to turn a current into a measurable voltage.

sections.heading: Capacitors - charge storage, filtering and timing
sections.body:
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field held between two conducting plates separated by an insulating dielectric. No charge crosses the gap; instead, electrons pile onto one plate and are repelled from the other, so the device behaves as though current passes through it whenever the voltage is changing. Capacitance C is measured in farads, but practical values are microfarads (uF, 10^-6), nanofarads (nF, 10^-9) and picofarads (pF, 10^-12). Four relations describe the behaviour. Q = C x V gives stored charge in coulombs. I = C x dV/dt says the current is proportional to the rate of voltage change, not to voltage itself. E = 0.5 x C x V^2 gives stored energy in joules. And for a simple parallel-plate geometry, C = epsilon0 x epsilon_r x A / d, where epsilon0 is 8.854 x 10^-12 farads per metre, epsilon_r is the dielectric's relative permittivity, A is plate area in square metres and d the separation in metres. That last equation explains why high-capacitance parts use enormous rolled or etched plate areas and vanishingly thin dielectrics.

The defining consequence is that a capacitor blocks steady DC and passes AC, with an opposition called reactance that falls as frequency rises: Xc = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C), in ohms. A 1 uF capacitor presents 1,592 ohms at 100 Hz but only 1.59 ohms at 100 kHz, which is why one placed across a power rail is nearly invisible to the DC supply yet a near short-circuit to high-frequency noise.

Pair a capacitor with a resistor and you get a clock. The time constant tau = R x C, in seconds, sets the pace: charging toward a supply V follows v(t) = V x (1 - e^(-t/tau)), reaching 63.2 percent of the target after one tau, 95 percent after three and 99.3 percent after five, so five time constants is treated as fully charged. Discharge mirrors it, v(t) = V x e^(-t/tau). A 10 kilohm resistor with a 100 uF capacitor gives tau = 10,000 x 100 x 10^-6 = 1.0 second, so a 5 V rail falls to 1.84 V in one second and is effectively flat after five.

Dielectric choice determines where a part belongs. Ceramic C0G or NP0 types are small, stable and low-loss, so they suit timing and radio-frequency work. X7R and especially Y5V ceramics pack far more capacitance into the same case but lose 20 to 80 percent of their nominal value under DC bias and across temperature, which makes Y5V unusable for timing. Electrolytics are polarised and span 1 uF to 10,000 uF cheaply, the stripe marking the negative terminal; reversing one makes it vent or burst. Film capacitors in polyester or polypropylene are stable, non-polarised and preferred for audio and mains snubbing. Supercapacitors reach whole farads at about 2.7 V for backup power. Derate voltage in every case: run an electrolytic at no more than 60 to 70 percent of its rating, and choose 105 degC parts over 85 degC anywhere warm, because electrolytic life roughly halves for each 10 degC rise in operating temperature.

sections.heading: Inductors and the reactive pair
sections.body:
An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field created by current flowing through a coil, making it the exact dual of a capacitor. Inductance L is measured in henries, with practical values in millihenries and microhenries. Its governing relation, V = L x dI/dt, says the voltage across the coil is proportional to the rate of change of current, mirroring the capacitor's I = C x dV/dt. Stored energy is E = 0.5 x L x I^2, and inductive reactance Xl = 2 x pi x f x L rises with frequency rather than falling. The practical summary is that an inductor resists changes in current: it passes DC freely and increasingly obstructs high-frequency AC.

That resistance to change has a violent corollary. Interrupt the current through an inductor abruptly and dI/dt becomes enormous, so the coil generates a back-emf spike that can reach hundreds of volts from a 12 V supply. This is the mechanism behind an ignition coil's spark, and it is also why switching a relay coil, solenoid or motor with an unprotected transistor destroys that transistor within a few operations. The standard cure is a flyback diode wired reverse-biased across the coil, cathode to the positive end, which gives the collapsing current a harmless circulating path and clamps the spike to roughly one diode drop above the supply.

Put an inductor and capacitor together and their opposite frequency behaviours cancel at one point. Resonance occurs where Xl equals Xc, at f_resonant = 1 / (2 x pi x sqrt(L x C)). With L = 100 uH and C = 100 pF the product is 1 x 10^-14, whose square root is 1 x 10^-7, giving f = 1 / (2 x pi x 1 x 10^-7) = 1.59 MHz, squarely in the AM broadcast band. That is precisely how a radio's tuned circuit selects one station from the thousands of signals arriving at the antenna: at resonance the LC pair presents a sharp impedance peak or dip, and everything off-frequency is attenuated.

Most everyday filtering, however, needs no inductor at all. A low-pass RC filter puts a resistor in series with the signal and a capacitor from the output node to ground, so high frequencies are shunted away while DC passes. Its corner frequency is f_c = 1 / (2 x pi x R x C). With R = 1.6 kilohm and C = 100 nF, f_c = 1 / (2 x pi x 1,600 x 1 x 10^-7) = 995 Hz. At the corner the output has fallen to 70.7 percent of the input, which is minus 3 decibels, and above it the response rolls off at 20 decibels per decade, meaning a tenfold increase in frequency brings a tenfold reduction in amplitude. Swap the two parts, putting the capacitor in series and the resistor to ground, and the same formula now describes a high-pass filter that blocks DC and passes the fast changes. The honest caveat is that a single RC section is a gentle filter; where a sharp boundary between passband and stopband is required, several sections or an active filter built around an amplifier is needed instead.

sections.heading: Diodes - one-way valves and their many jobs
sections.body:
A diode conducts in one direction only. Conventional current flows from the anode to the cathode, the end marked with a printed band, and reverse bias blocks it. The underlying physics is the semiconductor junction, described by the Shockley equation I = Is x (e^(V/(n x Vt)) - 1), where Is is the saturation current, n the ideality factor between 1 and 2, and Vt = kT/q is the thermal voltage, about 25.85 mV at 300 kelvin. The exponential in that expression is the practical point: current rises so steeply with voltage that, for design purposes, the diode is treated as having a fixed forward drop once conducting. A silicon signal or rectifier diode such as the 1N4148 or 1N4007 drops about 0.7 V. A Schottky such as the 1N5817 or BAT54 drops only 0.2 to 0.4 V and switches far faster, making it the right choice for low-voltage rectification and reverse-polarity protection. Germanium sits near 0.3 V. An LED drops 1.8 to 2.2 V for red and yellow, and 3.0 to 3.4 V for blue, white and green.

Three ratings determine survival: I_F, the maximum forward current; V_RRM, the peak repetitive reverse voltage, beyond which the junction avalanches; and reverse recovery time, which begins to matter above a few kilohertz because a slow diode keeps conducting briefly after the voltage reverses.

Four canonical jobs cover most uses. Rectification converts AC to DC: a full-wave bridge of four diodes delivers a peak of V_ac(rms) x 1.414 minus two diode drops, so a 12 V RMS transformer gives 12 x 1.414 = 16.97 V, minus 1.4 V, equals 15.6 V peak. A smoothing capacitor then holds that level between peaks, with ripple approximated by V_ripple = I_load / (f_ripple x C); for a 0.5 A load, 100 Hz ripple and 2,200 uF, that is 0.5 / (100 x 0.0022) = 2.27 V peak to peak. Freewheeling across an inductive load is the second job, absorbing the collapse spike from relays and motors. Reverse-polarity protection is the third, a Schottky in series with the supply wasting less headroom than silicon. The fourth is the Zener diode, deliberately operated in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage such as 3.3, 5.1 or 12 V to serve as a simple reference. A Zener must always be fed through a series resistor sized R = (V_in - V_z) / (I_z + I_load), and its dissipation P = V_z x I_z checked against the rating.

Driving an LED shows why the exponential curve demands respect. For a red LED with V_f = 2.0 V at I_f = 20 mA on a 5 V supply, the series resistor is R = (5 - 2.0) / 0.020 = 150 ohms, which happens to be a stocked E12 value exactly. Resistor dissipation is I^2 x R = 0.02^2 x 150 = 0.06 W, so a 0.125 W part is comfortable. Never connect an LED straight across a supply: a few tenths of a volt above its forward voltage produces destructive current, and the part fails within milliseconds.

sections.heading: Transistors - switching and amplification
sections.body:
A transistor lets a small signal control a much larger current, which is the single capability that makes amplifiers, logic gates and switching power supplies possible. Two families dominate practice, and they are controlled in fundamentally different ways.

The bipolar junction transistor, or BJT, is current controlled. It has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. An NPN device such as the 2N3904 or BC547 conducts from collector to emitter once the base sits roughly 0.7 V above the emitter; a PNP is the mirror image, conducting when the base is pulled 0.7 V below the emitter. The defining relations are I_C = beta x I_B and I_E = I_B + I_C. Beta, also printed as hFE, is the current gain, typically 100 to 300, but it varies by a factor of three between samples of the same part number and drifts with temperature and collector current. Never design a circuit whose behaviour depends on an exact beta.

A worked switching example makes the arithmetic concrete.
